title: Enhancing access in breast cancer prevention clinical trials
text:
Most individuals eligible for cancer prevention trials are not patients at a cancer center where these trials are
accessible. Identifying the framework to deliver breast cancer prevention clinical trials to the community could
improve access and representation of our communities in cancer prevention clinical trials.

title: Computational modulator design and machine learning to target protein-protein interactions
text:
Computational modulator design and machine learning to target protein-protein interactions
Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are functionally involved in every cellular signaling pathway. The
artificial modulation of PPIs represents a challenging but very promising direction in drug discovery. Here
we aim to develop new computational tools, state-of-the-art machine learning models and innovative design
strategies to overcome current limitations in computational aided drug design, and discover highly specific and
potent modulators of a variety of medically important biomolecular interactions as tools for studying biological
functions, as well as new leads for therapeutic development.

title: Genome editing of human pancreatic islets to withstand ischemic injuries and promote immune evasion
text:
Islet transplantation replaces the lost insulin-producing pancreatic islet beta cells due to type 1 diabetes.
However, this therapy is not widely used because of its variable efficacy and the requirement for life-long
immunosuppression that can lead to a whole host of problems. We will tackle these issues using genetic
engineering to help islet to withstand the stress of transplantation and resist immune attacks. The goal is to
develop strategy for highly efficient islet transplantation without the need of immunosuppression.

title: Neuroimaging and Vascular Core
text: Clinical neuroimaging of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) subjects is a critical aspect of understanding disease onset, progression, and response to therapies. The UCI MODEL-AD team is developing new mouse models of AD that more readily recapitulate the human disease. As new mouse models are generated by the Disease Model Development and Phenotyping Project (DMP), the Neuroimaging and Neurovascular Core (NIVC) will undertake a compendium of imaging modalities to deeply phenotype these mice using clinically relevant, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences to probe structure, tissue cellularity, and physiological functions in an age, sex and diet dependent manner. The NIVC will also undertake a novel vessel-painting approach that labels the cerebrovasculature. The goals of the NIVC are to significantly increase our structural and functional understanding of how the MODEL AD mouse brain responds to genetic perturbations reminiscent of human AD and to link these discoveries to clinical AD imaging. To accomplish these goals, we will undertake four Aims. Aim 1 is to determine deep MRI and vascular phenotypes for DMP base-platform mice and high-interest models. This Aim will use standardized (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative; ADNI-derived) and innovative multimodal MRI techniques to describe structural, vascular, structural/functional connectivity, and metabolic signatures in emerging AD mouse models. Aim 2 is to facilitate biomarker development by integrating MRI with histopathological and multi-omic data. Here, NIVC data will be merged with DMP and Functional Genomics Bioinformatics Data Management Core (FGBDMC) data to identify biomarker signatures on neuroimaging data that provides insights on the underlying AD neurobiology. Aim 3 will validate potential MRI biomarkers emerging from recent human AD studies, which include spectroscopic imaging and quantitative susceptibility mapping. Aim 4 is to disseminate MODEL-AD neuroimaging and vascular findings to the larger international AD community and to provide entry to new researchers interested in AD. In summary, the NIVC will: 1) innovate new imaging approaches for phenotyping mouse models and make these data publicly available for AD researchers, 2) collaborate with human and mouse neuroimaging groups to pursue evaluation of potential predictive markers that could guide early clinical diagnosis of AD, 3) educate the scientific (students, postdocs, new researchers) and the broader public community about AD, and, 4) translate the NIVC findings to provide new directions for neuroimaging approaches to aid diagnosis and monitor treatment response of human AD.

title: The combined role of ARID1A loss and estrogen signaling in endometrial cancer
text:
Estrogen signaling plays a critical role in the development of endometrial cancer; however, it may not be
sufficient to drive tumor formation as endometrial cancer usually arises in the context of common mutations
and excess estrogens. The goal of the project is to determine how ARID1A mutations, which are common in
endometrial tumors, cooperate with estrogen signaling and explore novel treatment strategies for the majority
of endometrial cancers, which have ARID1A alterations and active estrogen signaling.

title: 2026 Epithelial Stem Cells and Niches Gordon Research Conference and Gordon Research Seminar
text:
Understanding epithelial stem cell regulation within tissues will serve to repair or replace cells or organs
damaged by injury, disease, and aging. The strategies vary from generating cell types and tissues in a dish
for transplantation purposes to directly stimulating the damaged organ in the living organism. This field has
been exponentially growing for the past decade, and this conference will allow bringing together scientists
from currently disparate areas, which will create synergy and result in faster progress in this field that is
highly medically significant.

title: The biogenesis and functions of pre-meiotic small RNAs in male reproductive development in maize
text:
Plants express small RNAs that accumulate to high levels in reproductive organs harboring the
male germline; these small RNAs show interesting parallels to the animal piRNAs, and
perturbation of their biogenesis or activities causes sterility. Our proposed study aims to
understand the localization, biogenesis, functions, and targets of a specialized class of the small
RNAs (the 21-nt phased, small interfering RNAs) that are abundant prior to meiosis, using the
maize as the model system. The research outcomes will provide mechanistic insights into the
biogenesis and functions of these small RNAs, with the potential to illuminate why plants have
evolved this unusual small RNA pathway enriched in or even specific to male reproduction.

title: Identifying Factors in Hearing Healthcare Access: The Memphis SOUND Project
text:
Hearing loss is a significant public health issue that disproportionately affects Black older adults, who experience
higher rates of hearing-related comorbidities but lower use of hearing care. The Memphis SOUND Project will
partner with 10 faith-based organizations in Memphis to examine social, epidemiological, environmental, and
ecological factors that influence hearing healthcare access, using the PRECEDE-PROCEED Model and a Faith
Champion engagement approach. Findings will lay the groundwork for a scalable, community-driven intervention
that reduces the consequences of untreated hearing loss and advances hearing healthcare access across
populations.

title: Designing Engineered Stem Cell Therapies for Immune-Mediated Demyelinating Diseases
text:
Immune-mediated demyelinating diseases of the central nervous system affect over 5 million patients worldwide.
This proposal seeks to develop chimeric antigen receptor-engineered mesenchymal stem cell therapies that
better control disease by inhibiting immune system autoreactivity. The results from this research will help refine
clinical therapy and will have a direct impact on patient care.

title: Advancing Probe Technology for Ultrasensitive RNA Imaging via Hybridization Chain Reaction
text:
Advancing Probe Technology for Ultrasensitive RNA Imaging via Hybridization Chain Reaction
We propose to engineer and commercialize molecular technology that will enable simultaneous ultrasensitive
imaging of multiple RNA molecules of different classes within sample types critical to drug development, clinical
pathology, and biological research. The resulting products will enable the development of new therapies, the
clinical diagnosis of disease, and the study of human biology and disease.

title: 6/11 Astrocyte-specific changes and interventions in alcohol dependence
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health and to the NIAAA's mission because it employs novel
approaches to investigate neuroimmune factors expressed by astrocytes (understudied brain cells that are
essential for the proper functioning of the brain) in an animal model of alcohol dependence. The proposed
studies will provide insights on how alterations in astrocytes result in increased inflammation leading to
increased alcohol drinking. The aforementioned insights, obtained using

title: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity and the emergence of antibiotic resistance
text:
This proposal focuses on the initial steps in the emergence of antibiotic resistance, looking at how intrinsic
tolerance mechanisms may provide a window of protection that allows bacteria to acquire resistance via
horizontal gene transfer or mutation. The resulting data will be relevant for revealing novel routes by which
bacteria evade drug treatment and can inform treatment strategies to combat the spread of antibiotic
resistance.

title: Dissecting the in vivo stromal metabolic and inflammatory crosstalk in colorectal cancer
text:
The tumor microenvironment is a critical driver of cancer progression in colorectal cancer (CRC). Dr. Duran’s
application to the R50 Research Specialist Award will support Dr. Moscat’s research program focused on the role
of the tumor microenvironment in CRC. Unveiling the mechanisms that control this crosstalk is crucial to find new
therapeutic targets for CRC.

title: Targeting of Nicotinamide N Methyltransferase (NNMT) in the Tumor Microenvironment to Sensitize Cancer to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
text:
This project will develop a novel inhibitor of the enzyme NNMT and investigate its potential to improve
responses to immunotherapy in ovarian and colorectal cancers. By studying how NNMT inhibition remodels the
tumor microenvironment and enhances anti-PD-1 therapy, this work may lead to more effective treatments for
patients with immunotherapy-resistant solid tumors, directly addressing a major challenge in cancer care.

title: BioSystems Networks and Translational Research - Insights into Inflammation (BioSNTR-II)
text:
This proposed Center Of Biomedical Excellence is relevant for public health because it will improve molecular
and cellular mechanistic understanding of inflammatory processes. This work is relevant to the mission of NIH
in that the fundamental knowledge of inflammation generated by the center, will provide new strategies for
regulating inflammation in numerous disease states and inflammatory conditions.

title: Training in Drug Abuse and Brain Imaging
text:
Sophisticated brain imaging techniques are more frequently being used to better detect, understand, develop
new medications, and track and prevent drug abuse. Since its inception 19 years ago, we have built and
maintained an integrated, multidisciplinary Drug Abuse and Brain Imaging Training Program that currently
supports 4 postdoctoral slots to train postdoctoral fellows how to merge imaging technologies with basic and
applied clinical research and translational models of drug and alcohol abuse in order to meet these important
needs. The extensive breadth of credentials of program mentors offers our trainees the best opportunity to learn
to apply these skills in order to further our understanding of the neurobiological bases of the addicted brain.

title: Repetitive Stretch-Induced Myocardial Stiffening in Chronic Coronary Artery Disease
text:
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among Veterans and congestive heart failure, in particular,
is among the most common conditions resulting in death, disability, and hospitalization. Heart failure with
preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has emerged as the most common form of heart failure, but our poor
understanding of how it develops has made it difficult to devise effective treatments. The research proposed in
this application will address this problem by examining how repetitive stretch-induced remodeling of the non-
cellular components of heart muscle (i.e., the cardiac extracellular matrix) leads to persistent fibrotic collagen
deposition and a sustained reduction in cardiac compliance that promotes the development of HFpEF in patients
with chronic coronary artery disease (CAD). Improved understanding of this process is anticipated to reveal new
targets for therapies designed to prevent or reverse heart muscle stiffening in CAD patients at-risk of developing
HFpEF and significantly improve the quality of life and survival of Veterans with this common condition.

title: Leveraging North-South Partnerships toAdvance Cell and Gene Therapy for HIV Research Training Capacity in Uganda (C and GT-Uganda)
text:
Despite major advances in antiretroviral therapy, HIV remains a lifelong infection for approximately 40 million people globally, including more than one million individuals in the United States, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing most of the disease burden. Lifelong treatment presents ongoing challenges of adherence, long-term toxicity, resistance, and cost factors that also affect HIV care in the United States. Curative strategies based on cell and gene therapy (CGT) offer a transformative opportunity to overcome these challenges. Uganda provides a uniquely valuable scientific environment for advancing HIV cure research because of its large and well-characterized HIV cohorts, diverse viral subtypes, experienced clinical research infrastructure, and longstanding NIH-supported collaborations with U.S. investigators. These assets enable investigation of HIV reservoirs, immune responses, and therapeutic interventions in populations underrepresented in U.S.-based studies, thereby improving the relevance, safety, and effectiveness of CGT approaches intended for diverse patient populations, including Americans living with HIV. Research conducted in Uganda also enables more efficient evaluation of scalable and implementation-ready cure strategies that can inform future U.S. clinical applications.
This training program, Leveraging North–South Partnerships to Advance Cell and Gene Therapy for HIV Research Training Capacity in Uganda (CGT-Uganda), develops sustainable research and workforce capacity for CGT-based HIV cure research through a structured collaboration between Ugandan institutions and leading U.S. research centres. The program will train degree and non-degree fellows through integrated didactic coursework, mentored research, hands-on laboratory experience, and bilateral exchange placements at U.S. partner institutions, building expertise in CGT research, translational science, clinical-trial readiness, regulatory science, and ethical oversight.
By developing highly trained Ugandan investigators who can serve as long-term collaborators in NIH-funded studies and future multinational clinical trials, the program expands the research capacity available to U.S. investigators, accelerates scientific discovery, and enhances the global applicability of HIV cure strategies. This collaborative model directly advances U.S. scientific leadership in HIV cure research while supporting global efforts to reduce the long-term burden of HIV.

title: Imaging Research
text: IMAGING RESEARCH SHARED RESOURCE PROJECT SUMMARY / ABSTRACT The mission of the Imaging Research Shared Resource (Imaging SR) has been to provide all regional cancer investigators with comprehensive preclinical and clinical imaging capabilities and services to deliver in vivo and in situ imaging assessments of cancer. Established in 2005, the Imaging SR has now grown to become a multi- institutional SR with two sites at Case Western Reserve (CWRU)/University Hospitals (UH) and Cleveland Clinic (CC) integrating comprehensive, state-of-the-art imaging capabilities for both animal models of cancer (CWRU/UH and CC sites), as well as pediatric and adult patients (CWRU/UH site). The Imaging SR is supported by a well-established operational and administrative infrastructure including centralized imaging facilities at each site led by Flask, Chen and Androjna (Co-Directors) and supported by 9 highly-skilled Imaging SR staff with over 100 years of combined imaging expertise. The aims of the Imaging SR are to provide both imaging services and training on state-of-the-art imaging systems to all regional cancer investigators including: 1) high-volume preclinical bioluminescence and fluorescence imaging services; 2) custom-designed radionuclides for preclinical PET imaging capabilities to assess tumor progression, therapy, and metabolism; 3) novel in situ cryo- fluorescence imaging to direct cell/gene therapies; 4) MRI and MR Fingerprinting assessments for both mouse cancer models and cancer patients. Importantly, imaging services at both sites are available to all regional investigators through established, compliant inter-institutional agreements and operational processes. The capabilities and services provided by the Imaging SR have significantly expanded during the current funding cycle through investments by regional institutions, the NIH, and industrial collaborators including: 1) two new research-dedicated Siemens Vida 3T human MRI scanners (CWRU/UH site, ~$5M investment by CWRU/UH and Siemens); 2) a new Cubresa PET insert for the first small animal PET-MRI in the region (CWRU/UH site, ~$400K from NIH S10 award); 3) an upgraded 9.4T small animal MRI scanner supporting MR Fingerprinting development (CWRU/UH site, ~$1.1M investment by CWRU); 4) a new Mediso nanoscan PET/CT (CC site, ~$900K from NIH S10 award); and 5) a new Vevo F2 rodent ultrasound to support novel nanobubble development (CWRU/UH site, ~$400K investment by CWRU). The custom radiochemistry synthesis capabilities provided by the CWRU/UH site are also available to both sites to support novel preclinical PET imaging studies.

title: Elucidating roles and mechanisms of double-stranded RNA-mediated pathways
text:
Many animals, including humans, encode and express long noncoding double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Aberrant
regulation of this endogenous dsRNA is implicated as causative in disease, but also beneficial in some forms of
cancer. The proposed research will advance understanding of the mechanisms of these dsRNA-mediated
pathways.
